presentingComplaint: Two episodes of transient loss of consciousness while walking to the bathroom, with several weeks of unusual breathlessness and fatigue on exertion.
history: Frail 82-year-old woman brought by her daughter after a witnessed collapse while climbing the stairs; she went pale, slumped, was unresponsive for about 20 seconds, then recovered fully within a minute without confusion, incontinence or tongue-biting. A similar exertional 'greying-out' spell occurred 3 weeks earlier and was dismissed as dehydration. She denies palpitations, chest heaviness at rest, or a preceding aura, but on close questioning admits mild pressure-like exertional chest discomfort that she attributed to 'old age'. Over 2 months she has become breathless walking on the flat and now sleeps on two pillows. Background: long-standing hypertension, type 2 diabetes, mild CKD. She was told years ago of a 'heart murmur' but never had an echocardiogram. No recent GI blood loss, no vomiting, medications recently unchanged. The classic dramatic exertional syncope is muted here - the presentation is dominated by nonspecific fatigue and near-syncope in a frail elderly woman, and the murmur is soft and easily missed.
examination: Comfortable at rest, not distressed. Small-volume, slow-rising (parvus et tardus) carotid pulse. Apex beat sustained and non-displaced. A grade 2/6 ejection systolic murmur is heard at the right upper sternal edge radiating faintly to the carotids; the murmur is deceptively soft and the A2 component of the second heart sound is diminished. Late-peaking character on careful auscultation. Bibasal fine crackles. No focal neurology, no postural BP drop reproduced, tongue and continence intact.

labs.troponin: mildly elevated (16 ng/L, stable on serial testing)

imaging: ECG: sinus rhythm with LVH by voltage criteria and secondary repolarisation changes; no acute ST-elevation, no complete heart block. Chest X-ray: mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette with upper-lobe venous diversion, no calcified aorta commented on. Transthoracic echocardiogram: heavily calcified aortic valve with severely restricted leaflet opening; aortic valve area 0.8 cm2, dimensionless index 0.22, peak velocity 4.3 m/s, mean gradient 46 mmHg; concentric LV hypertrophy with preserved ejection fraction and impaired relaxation - findings diagnostic of severe aortic stenosis.
microbiology: Not applicable; blood cultures not indicated (afebrile, non-infective presentation).
differentialDiagnoses: Severe calcific aortic stenosis with exertional syncope (leading diagnosis)
Arrhythmic syncope (paroxysmal AF or conduction disease)
finalDiagnosis: Severe calcific aortic stenosis presenting with exertional (near-)syncope, dyspnoea and heart failure in a frail elderly woman - an atypical, soft-murmur presentation.
citations: ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease 2020/2021
ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Valvular Heart Disease (Aortic Stenosis) & Syncope
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective cardiac diagnosis; no antimicrobial therapy indicated.
contraindications: Avoid vasodilators/nitrates (ACE inhibitors, GTN) which can precipitate profound hypotension and syncope in fixed severe AS
Avoid aggressive diuresis or volume depletion - preload-dependent LV in AS
Avoid negatively inotropic/chronotropic agents that reduce cardiac output
Caution: soft murmur and low troponin can falsely reassure - severity is often underestimated in the elderly and in low-flow states
edgeCases: Low-flow, low-gradient severe AS with preserved EF may show a lower mean gradient despite a critically small valve area - do not exclude severe AS on gradient alone
A quiet murmur with soft/absent A2 can indicate more severe, not milder, disease
Exertional syncope in severe AS is an urgent indication for aortic valve replacement (surgical or TAVI) referral
expectedMaiK: Exertional syncope plus dyspnoea in an elderly patient with a slow-rising pulse, soft late-peaking ejection systolic murmur and diminished A2 should trigger urgent echocardiography for severe aortic stenosis; the softness of the murmur must not be falsely reassuring, and vasodilators must be avoided.
expectedNextQuestions: Is the syncope exertional and effort-related (versus postural or situational)?
Any associated exertional chest pressure or breathlessness suggesting the AS triad?
Character of the carotid pulse (parvus et tardus) and audibility of A2?
Prior murmur history and any previous echocardiogram?
Medications that lower preload/afterload (nitrates, ACE inhibitors, diuretics)?
expectedInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography (aortic valve area, peak velocity, mean gradient, LV function)
Serial troponin to exclude ACS mimic
Basic metabolic panel and full blood count
